h1: The 6 Best Tabletop Patio Heaters of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Tabletop Patio Heaters: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 propane tabletop patio heaters compared on BTU output, tank options, safety shutoffs and flame display for small outdoor areas.
summary: The Cuisinart 11,000 BTU tabletop heater is the best all-rounder, with an adjustable burner, an anti-tilt shutoff and a screen guard. The PrimeGlo does nearly the same for $50 to $100 and lets you hook up a 20 lb tank for long evenings. The Uniflasy 2-in-1 doubles as a fire bowl, while the Tangkula pyramid is the style pick for a small balcony.
intro: Tabletop patio heaters are sold on BTU, and the number misleads. Eleven thousand BTU sounds like a lot, but a tabletop unit warms an area of about 30 sq ft, roughly the radius of two or three chairs around it. That is a different job from a freestanding heater, which throws heat across a whole patio. Buy one to warm a conversation, not a yard.

We ranked six propane tabletop heaters on the Primea framework, weighting output, safety shutoffs, fuel flexibility and how well each fits a small table. Because open-flame heaters belong outdoors in open air, every review also notes the safety features the spec sheet actually lists, from anti-tilt protection to flameout valves.

products.name: Cuisinart Portable Tabletop Patio Heater, 11,000 BTU
products.verdict: 11,000 BTU, up to 30 sq ft, anti-tilt shutoff and a burner screen guard on a reflector plate.
products.description:
Output is 11,000 BTU from a propane burner with adjustable heat and a reflector top plate, warming up to 30 sq ft. Safety features listed are an anti-tilt shutoff and a burner screen guard.

It wins by listing the most safety detail: a guard that keeps a stray napkin from the burner is a feature you notice only when you need it. The Mars Explo and PrimeGlo match the BTU number, but this one pairs it with the clearest coverage and guard information.

Buy it for two or three people on a patio table. The caveat is the $100 to $200 price, and the tank sits low, so keep it on a stable surface.
products.idealFor: Anyone who wants straightforward warmth for two or three people with clear safety features.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest price or a fire-bowl look.

products.name: PrimeGlo Portable Tabletop Patio Heater, 11,000 BTU
products.verdict: Runs on a 1 lb tank or a 20 lb tank through a 5 ft adapter hose, in a hammered silver finish.
products.description:
The PrimeGlo delivers 11,000 BTU with variable control and anti-tilt protection. It takes a 1 lb tank or, with the 5 ft adapter hose, a 20 lb tank.

It ranks second because the 20 lb option fixes the main annoyance of tabletop heaters: a 1 lb canister empties quickly. At $50 to $100 it costs less than the Cuisinart, though its listing gives no coverage figure or guard detail.

Buy it for hosting, with a large tank hidden under the table. The caveat is the hose, which you must route and secure away from feet.

keySpecs.label: Fuel
keySpecs.value: 1 lb tank, or 20 lb with adapter hose

products.idealFor: Hosts who want the option of a 20 lb tank for evenings that run long.
products.skipIf: You want a stated burner guard.

products.name: Uniflasy 2-in-1 Tabletop Patio Heater and Fire Pit
products.verdict: A 13,000 BTU fire bowl above an 8,000 BTU radiant burner, each with its own knob.
products.description:
Two burners stack here: a 13,000 BTU upper fire bowl with 2.2 lb of glass beads, and an 8,000 BTU lower radiant burner, with two independent knobs and a piezo ignition. It connects to 1, 20 or 30 lb cylinders.

That makes it the highest total output in the group at $50 to $100, and the only one that doubles as a fire feature. It ranks third because the tabletop footprint is bigger than the single-burner models, and two burners at once draw fuel quickly.

Buy it for a roomy table where you want a flame and heat control. The caveat is fuel use, so connect a larger tank.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a fire-pit look and separate heat control on a roomy table.
products.skipIf: You have a small bistro table.

products.name: Tangkula Tabletop Propane Patio Heater, 11,000 BTU
products.verdict: A steel and aluminum 11,000 BTU heater with an ignition switch, control knob and tip-over protection.
products.description:
Output is 11,000 BTU from a steel and aluminum body, with an ignition switch plus control knob, an adjustable flame and tip-over protection.

It ranks fourth because it matches the Cuisinart on output without the guard or coverage detail, and it matches the PrimeGlo without the 20 lb option. The switch-and-knob start is the plain, quick way to light a heater when guests are waiting.

Buy it for simplicity. The caveat is the $100 to $200 price without extras.
products.idealFor: People who prioritize a simple switch-and-knob start over styling extras.
products.skipIf: You want a 20 lb tank option.

products.name: Mars Explo Tabletop Patio Heater, 11,000 BTU
products.verdict: A real flame in a quartz glass tube, auto shutoff and an anti-tilt base for balconies and porches.
products.description:
Output is 11,000 BTU with coverage up to 30 sq ft, a real flame in a quartz glass tube, auto shutoff and an anti-tilt base. The listing names commercial, balcony and porch settings.

It ranks fifth because the glass tube puts style ahead of heat: the flame is visible, but the burner is less open than a plain reflector design. Against the Cuisinart it offers similar coverage for the same $100 to $200 with less safety detail.

Buy it for the look of a flame at the table. The caveat is that glass gets hot, so keep hands away.

keySpecs.label: Flame
keySpecs.value: Real flame in quartz glass tube

products.idealFor: Anyone who wants a visible flame in a glass tube as part of the table setting.
products.skipIf: You prefer an open reflector design.

products.name: Tangkula 34 in Pyramid Tabletop Patio Heater, 9,500 BTU
products.verdict: A 34 inch bronze pyramid with a crystal glass tube, flameout protection and 9,500 BTU.
products.description:
Rated 9,500 BTU, the Tangkula pyramid stands 34 inches tall in a bronze 430 stainless steel frame with a crystal glass tube. Protections are tip-over and flameout, plus a safety valve.

It ranks last because 9,500 BTU is the lowest output here and the tall frame is a bigger commitment than the other tabletop models. The flameout protection is the most thorough safety wording, but it does not make up for the lower heat.

Buy it for a small space where the classic pyramid look matters. The caveat is that 34 inches is tall for a table.
products.idealFor: Small spaces where you want the classic pyramid look at tabletop scale.
products.skipIf: Heat output matters more than looks.

whatMatters.detail: BTU measures heat output, but a tabletop unit warms a small radius. The Cuisinart and Mars Explo list up to 30 sq ft at 11,000 BTU. Treat that as two or three chairs, and do not buy one expecting to warm a whole deck.

Propane heaters should include anti-tilt or tip-over protection. The Tangkula pyramid adds flameout protection and a safety valve, and the Cuisinart a burner screen guard. These features matter most on a table where a bump is likely, so read the safety line before you read the price, and confirm the shutoff is described in plain words rather than implied by a photo.

A 1 lb canister runs out fast on a tabletop heater. The PrimeGlo accepts a 20 lb tank through a 5 ft hose and the Uniflasy 1, 20 or 30 lb cylinders. If you entertain often, a large-tank option saves refills mid-evening.

Propane heaters belong outdoors in open air. Even those labeled for balcony use, such as the Mars Explo, should not be used in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces. Check your building's rules on balcony propane before buying.

The Tangkula pyramid stands 34 inches tall and the Uniflasy stacks two burners. Measure your table, and keep clear space around the heater. A heater on a wobbly or tiny table defeats every safety feature on the spec sheet, so test the table with a firm push first.

faq.q: Can I use these on a wooden table?
faq.a: Use a heat-resistant surface or a trivet. The Cuisinart and PrimeGlo throw heat downward from a reflector or burner, which can scorch wood. Keep clearance from tablecloths and umbrellas, and never use any of them in a closed space.

faq.q: What mistake do people make with tabletop heaters?
faq.a: Expecting patio-wide warmth. At 11,000 BTU and about 30 sq ft, the Cuisinart and Mars Explo warm the people seated around the table. A larger area needs a freestanding heater, not more tabletop units. Check the stated coverage on the listing, and be wary of any model that omits it.

faq.q: Is the Cuisinart worth it over the PrimeGlo?
faq.a: If you value the screen guard and stated coverage. The Cuisinart lists them, while the PrimeGlo offers a 20 lb tank option for $50 to $100 less. For long evenings, many buyers will prefer the PrimeGlo.

faq.q: How do I connect a 20 lb tank?
faq.a: The PrimeGlo includes a 5 ft adapter hose, and the Uniflasy takes 20 or 30 lb cylinders. Connect only with the correct regulator, check for leaks with soapy water, and keep the tank upright and out of foot traffic.

faq.q: How do I maintain a tabletop heater?
faq.a: Let it cool, then wipe the reflector and glass. Keep the burner clear of debris and spider webs, which can block gas flow. Store the Tangkula or Mars Explo indoors in winter, with the propane disconnected.

faq.q: Can I use the Uniflasy as a fire pit only?
faq.a: Yes, the upper 13,000 BTU burner works as a fire bowl with glass beads, while the lower 8,000 BTU burner is the radiant heater. Each has its own knob, so you can run either independently.

finalTake: The Cuisinart Portable Tabletop Patio Heater, 11,000 BTU is the best pick for most people thanks to its guard and shutoff, while the PrimeGlo gives nearly the same heat for less money plus a 20 lb tank option. Choose the Uniflasy if you want a fire bowl, the Mars Explo for visible flame, and the Tangkula pyramid for style. Always use them outdoors in open air.
